title: Offline evals tell you if it can work. Production evals tell you if it is working.
linkedin_md:
# Offline evals tell you if it can work. Production evals tell you if it is working.

Most teams start with offline evals because they are the fastest way to get signal.

You collect a dataset, define expected behavior, run model or prompt variants, and compare scores. Maybe you grade with exact match, rubric-based LLM judges, human review, or task-specific checks. You get a table. Variant B beats Variant A by 7%. Ship it.

That is useful.

It is also incomplete.

Offline evals answer a narrow question: given the examples we already know how to test, does this system produce acceptable outputs in a controlled environment?

Production evals answer a different question: given real users, real traffic, real latency, real tool failures, real distribution shift, and real business constraints, is the system behaving well enough to keep serving?

You need both because they catch different failures.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## Offline evals are for iteration speed

Offline evals are where you should be doing most of your early model and prompt work.

They are cheap, repeatable, and debuggable. If you are choosing between two prompts, two retrieval strategies, or two tool-selection policies, you do not want to wait three days for production data. You want a harness that runs in minutes.

A good offline eval set should include at least three buckets:

1. Golden path examples, where the system should obviously succeed.
2. Edge cases, where previous versions failed or where the task is ambiguous.
3. Negative cases, where the correct behavior is refusal, clarification, escalation, or no action.

For LLM systems, the negative cases matter more than teams expect. Most production incidents are not "the answer was slightly worse." They are "the system confidently did the wrong thing when it should have stopped."

Offline evals are also where you test regressions.

If your agent handles 20 common workflows, each workflow should have locked examples. When you change the planner, add a tool, upgrade the model, or rewrite the system prompt, you should know whether workflow 7 broke before users do.

The tradeoff: offline evals are only as good as the distribution they cover.

A 500-example eval can be valuable. A 5,000-example eval can still miss the actual failure mode users hit tomorrow. Coverage is not just size. Coverage is whether your examples represent meaningful behavior boundaries.

## Production evals are for reality

Production evals start after deployment, but they should be designed before deployment.

They measure what actually happens under live conditions. That includes user phrasing, retries, timeouts, bad inputs, missing context, permission issues, retrieval drift, tool API changes, and unexpected task combinations.

A production eval system usually needs several layers.

First, log the right traces. For agentic systems, final output is not enough. You need intermediate decisions: retrieved documents, tool calls, tool responses, planner steps, confidence signals, latency, token usage, fallback paths, and whether the user corrected the system.

Second, define online quality signals. Some are explicit, like thumbs up, thumbs down, user ratings, or human review. Some are implicit, like task completion, abandonment, repeated rephrasing, manual override, escalation, or undo rate.

Third, sample for review. You will not manually inspect every trace. But you can review 50 to 200 representative sessions per week, stratified by task type, model version, high-cost calls, low-confidence cases, and user complaints.

Fourth, monitor guardrail metrics. Examples: tool error rate above 2%, p95 latency above 12 seconds, fallback rate doubling week over week, retrieval returning zero documents for common intents, or judge scores dropping after a model migration.

These numbers are not universal. They depend on the product. But every production LLM system needs thresholds where the team agrees, "if this moves, we investigate."

## They fail in opposite directions

Offline evals can make you overconfident.

The model sees clean test cases. Inputs are normalized. The right answer exists. The evaluator knows what good looks like. The system is not under load. Tools respond. Users do not change their mind halfway through.

Production evals can make you noisy.

Real users are messy. Some requests are impossible. Some feedback is wrong. Some failures are caused by upstream systems. Some "bad" outputs are actually reasonable responses to underspecified prompts.

That is why neither should be treated as the source of truth alone.

Offline evals are better for controlled comparisons. If model A beats model B on a stable eval by 8 points across 1,000 examples, that is meaningful.

Production evals are better for detecting unknown unknowns. If users are abandoning a workflow 30% more often after launch, your offline score does not matter until you understand why.

## The loop that works

The best teams connect the two.

When production review finds a failure, they turn it into an offline eval. Not every single bad trace, but every meaningful class of failure.

If users ask multi-intent questions and the agent only handles the first intent, add examples. If retrieval misses documents with synonyms, add examples. If the system calls tools when it should ask a clarification question, add examples. If a new model becomes more verbose and breaks downstream parsing, add examples.

Production finds the bug class. Offline evals prevent it from coming back.

This is especially important for agents because their failures are often path-dependent. The final answer may look plausible, but the system may have selected the wrong tool, skipped verification, used stale context, or taken an expensive route for a simple task.

For agents, evaluate trajectories, not just outputs.

A production trace might reveal that the final answer was correct, but the agent made 9 tool calls when 2 were enough. That matters. Cost and latency are product quality.

## Do not hide behind one score

A single aggregate eval score is usually too blunt.

Break scores down by task type, input difficulty, user segment, tool path, language, retrieval-needed versus no-retrieval, and refusal-needed versus answer-needed.

A system that scores 86% overall might be 96% on common happy paths and 42% on high-risk edge cases. The average hides the part that can hurt you.

Also separate quality from reliability.

Quality asks: was the answer good?

Reliability asks: did the system complete the workflow without infrastructure failure, timeout, malformed output, invalid tool call, or missing dependency?

A model upgrade might improve quality and reduce reliability. A prompt change might improve refusals and hurt task completion. You need enough metrics to see the tradeoff.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## Takeaways

Use offline evals before shipping. They are your fast iteration loop, regression suite, and model comparison tool.

Use production evals after shipping. They are your reality check, drift detector, and source of new failure cases.

Do not expect offline evals to predict every production issue. Do not expect production metrics to explain failures without trace review.

For LLM agents, evaluate both final outputs and trajectories. Tool choice, intermediate reasoning artifacts, latency, cost, retries, and escalation behavior all matter.

The practical loop is simple:

1. Build an offline eval for known behavior.
2. Ship with production tracing and monitoring.
3. Review real failures every week.
4. Convert recurring failure classes into offline tests.
5. Repeat before every major model, prompt, retrieval, or tool change.

Offline evals tell you whether the system can work.

Production evals tell you whether it keeps working when users show up.
